screens.title: Access Control, Front-running, and Tx.origin
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore three practical classes of smart contract risks: incorrect access control that uses the wrong caller identity, front-running attacks where an adversary races transactions, and denial-of-service vectors that make functions unusable. You will learn the concrete difference between msg. sender and tx. origin, why using tx. origin for authorization can be exploited via a phishing-style malicious relay, and how to use msg. sender and established patterns like onlyOwner to avoid that trap. We’ll then examine front-running in time-sensitive operations and walk through mitigations such as commit-reveal, batching or delaying execution, and limiting slippage for trades. Finally, we’ll investigate DoS attacks driven by unbounded loops or blocking external calls and practical defenses like pagination, pull-over-push withdrawals, and designing state changes to tolerate failing external calls. Each topic includes a code example and testing approach so you can both fix vulnerable code and write tests that assert the protection. By the end, you should be able to identify these issues in code, patch them safely, and structure tests that prove the contract resists simple exploit scenarios. Ask yourself: which caller identity are you trusting, and could an intermediate contract be tricking your logic?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Overview
Access Control, Front-running, Tx.origin
A focused, practical tour of caller identity mistakes, mempool races, and DoS loops with code-first examples and testing advice.
In this lesson

You’ll learn the difference between msg.sender and tx.origin, see a phishing relay exploit, patch it using msg.sender or onlyOwner, study front-running mitigations like commit-reveal and batching, and identify DoS vectors such as unbounded loops and blocking external calls.

Why it matters

These vulnerabilities can lead to stolen funds, unfair market advantage, or a contract becoming permanently unusable. Small design choices have large security consequences.

Explore Key Topics
Caller identity
Why msg.sender is the immediate caller and tx.origin is the original EOA — and why you should not authorize with tx.origin.
Front-running
How mempool visibility enables attackers to reorder transactions and practical mitigations used in auctions and DEXes.
Denial-of-Service
Gas-limit attacks and blocking withdrawals; use pagination and pull over push to reduce DoS surface.
Visual Concept
Cards show the attack surface and common mitigations
Risk
Trusting the wrong caller or exposing time-sensitive info creates easy exploit paths.
Fix
Use msg.sender-based checks, explicit modifiers, commit-reveal for secrecy, and pull-over-push for payments.
Coming up
We begin by clarifying caller identities, then show vulnerable code, an exploit, how to patch it, and tests to prove the patch works.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will be able to identify and fix common access control mistakes, understand and mitigate front-running, and design contracts that resist denial-of-service vectors. First, you will clearly distinguish msg. sender from tx. origin and explain why relying on tx. origin for authorization is unsafe. Second, you will name at least two front-running mitigations and reason about when to apply commit-reveal versus batching or slippage limits. Third, you will recognize DoS patterns such as unbounded loops and blocking external calls and apply defenses like pagination and pull-over-push. Finally, you will implement tests that simulate these attacks: use unauthorized accounts to assert reverts, deploy a malicious relay contract to reproduce a tx. origin phishing exploit, and create large data sets to verify loops can exceed gas limits. These skills matter because they let you move from reactive fixes to proactive design: you can write contracts that remain usable under adversarial conditions and write tests that demonstrate resilience. Think about your current contracts and ask: which functions would fail if an attacker filled an array, or if a user was tricked into calling a malicious relay?

screens.title: Learning Objectives (continued)
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practical habits you should adopt. First, always prefer msg. sender for immediate caller checks and wrap sensitive functions with a clear modifier, for example an onlyOwner pattern. Second, when a function’s correctness depends on secrecy or timing—like auction bids or large DEX trades—apply a commit-reveal workflow or batching so attackers cannot observe and profit from pending transactions. Third, use pull-over-push withdrawals and guard loops against unbounded growth to prevent DoS. Finally, integrate tests that mimic an attacker: deploy a malicious relay contract that calls your vulnerable function when the victim interacts, and run large-scale tests that populate arrays to see whether operations run out of gas. These behaviors reduce the chance that a design decision creates a simple exploit. When reviewing code, ask: who am I trusting, what data is visible in the mempool, and what happens if an external call reverts?

screens.title: msg.sender vs tx.origin
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s clearly define the two caller identities you’ll see in Solidity. msg. sender is the address that immediately invoked the current call. If an EOA calls your contract directly, msg. sender is that EOA. But if a contract calls your contract, msg. sender is the intermediary contract. tx. origin, by contrast, is the original externally owned account that began the entire transaction chain. That difference matters because tx. origin remains the same through nested calls, which means a malicious contract can cause tx. origin to be an honest user while msg. sender is the attacker-controlled contract. A concrete example: a contract that uses require(tx. origin == owner) to protect a withdraw function can be drained if the owner is tricked into calling a malicious relay. The relay’s call will have msg. sender equal to the relay, but tx. origin equal to the owner, satisfying the check. A common misconception is thinking tx. origin is a stronger identity because it ties back to the original user; in fact it opens a phishing vector because you no longer control who can place an intermediary contract between the EOA and your contract. The safe rule is: authorize the immediate caller you expect. Use msg. sender or explicit modifiers like onlyOwner, and test your assumptions by deploying a relay contract in your test suite. Takeaway: prefer msg. sender-based checks and treat tx. origin as unsafe for authorization.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › msg.sender vs tx.origin
Definition & contrast
msg.sender
The immediate caller of the current contract. It could be an EOA or another contract. This is the value you should validate for access control.
tx.origin
The original externally owned account that started the transaction. It does not change through nested calls, which makes it unsafe for authorization checks.
Common misconception
Believing tx.origin is a more trustworthy identifier because it ties to a human user. In reality, this allows a malicious intermediary to trick that user into authorizing unintended calls.
Key Takeaway

Always validate msg.sender for access checks and wrap critical functions with an explicit modifier like onlyOwner.

Concrete example
// Vulnerable access using tx.origin
function withdrawFunds() public {
    require(tx.origin == owner, "Only owner can withdraw"); // Vulnerable!
    // ... logic to withdraw funds ...
}

// Safe pattern uses msg.sender and a modifier
modifier onlyOwner() {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function");
    _;
}

function withdrawFunds() public onlyOwner { /* ... */ }
This code shows why tx.origin allows a phishing relay to pass the owner check. Testing with a malicious relay confirms the exploit.
Pro-tip: add unit tests that deploy a relay contract and simulate the victim calling it; assert that msg.sender-based checks block the call while tx.origin checks do not.

screens.title: Vulnerable Wallet: tx.origin Exploit
screens.narratorSegment: Now we examine a concrete vulnerable contract that uses tx. origin for an authorization check. The VulnerableWalletTxOrigin contract sets owner to the deployer and then requires tx. origin == owner for a transfer function. That condition looks like it protects the owner, but it doesn't restrict intermediate callers. An attacker can deploy a separate malicious relay contract that calls transferTo on the vulnerable wallet. If the owner is tricked into calling the relay’s function—perhaps by interacting with a dApp or a phishing link—the transaction's tx. origin stays the owner, while msg. sender becomes the relay contract. The relay then calls transferTo and passes the tx. origin check, enabling funds to move to the attacker. This is more than theory: we can reproduce it in tests by deploying the vulnerable wallet with an initial balance, deploying the malicious relay by the attacker, then having the owner call the relay's phishing function. The test should assert that the attacker's balance in the wallet increases and the owner's decreases. A common misconception is thinking that only contracts can be malicious; EOAs can be tricked into initiating a transaction chain that hands access to an attacker. The takeaway is to never rely on tx. origin for authorization and to write tests that intentionally try the relay scenario.

keyIdea.title: Vulnerability explained
keyIdea.text: Using tx.origin for access control allows a malicious relay to cause an owner-initiated transaction to authorize an attack.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Vulnerable Wallet
VulnerableWalletTxOrigin.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract VulnerableWalletTxOrigin {
    address public owner;
    mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

    constructor() payable {
        owner = msg.sender;
        balances[owner] = msg.value;
    }

    function deposit() public payable {
        balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
    }

    // Vulnerable function: uses tx.origin for access control
    function transferTo(address _to, uint256 _amount) public {
        require(tx.origin == owner, "Only the original owner can transfer"); // Vulnerable!
        require(balances[owner] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");
        balances[owner] -= _amount;
        balances[_to] += _amount;
    }

    function getBalance(address _addr) public view returns (uint256) {
        return balances[_addr];
    }
}
This code initializes the owner and keeps simple balances, but the transferTo check uses tx.origin. That allows a malicious intermediary to call transferTo while the owner is the originating EOA, bypassing intended restrictions.
Attack pattern
  • Attacker deploys a relay contract that calls transferTo on the vulnerable wallet.
  • Victim (the owner) is tricked into calling the relay, perhaps by a phishing interaction.
  • tx.origin remains the victim, so the transfer passes and funds move to the attacker.
Common mistake
Assuming the original user is proof that the call is authorized. The intermediate contract is under attacker control.

screens.title: Malicious Relay: How the Phishing Attack Works
screens.narratorSegment: Next we inspect the malicious relay contract used to trick an owner into authorizing a transfer. The relay receives the target vulnerable wallet address at deployment and stores the attacker as the deployer. Its phishingAttack function simply calls the vulnerable wallet’s transfer function while the owner, acting as the origin, triggers the relay. This demonstrates the exact sequence in which tx. origin remains the owner while msg. sender is the relay. In practice, an attacker will try to induce the owner to call the relay—for example by promising some benefit or by social engineering—so tests should simulate the owner calling the relay directly. You should be able to reproduce this attack in unit tests: deploy the vulnerable wallet with an initial balance, deploy the malicious relay by the attacker, then call phishingAttack connected as the owner. Assertions must check that the attacker’s wallet balance increased inside the vulnerable wallet and the owner’s decreased. A misconception to avoid is thinking only on-chain bots can perform these steps; the owner themselves can trigger the chain when interacting with a malicious dApp. The defensive lesson is to assume intermediaries can exist and to protect the immediate caller, not the origin.

keyIdea.title: Relay mechanism
keyIdea.text: A malicious relay makes the owner the tx.origin while the relay is the direct caller, allowing tx.origin checks to be bypassed.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Malicious Relay
MaliciousRelay.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

import "./VulnerableWalletTxOrigin.sol";

contract MaliciousRelay {
    VulnerableWalletTxOrigin public targetWallet;
    address public attacker;

    constructor(address _targetWalletAddress) {
        targetWallet = VulnerableWalletTxOrigin(_targetWalletAddress);
        attacker = msg.sender; // Attacker is the deployer of this malicious contract
    }

    // This function is meant to trick the owner into calling it
    function phishingAttack(address _victim, uint256 _amount) public {
        // When the victim (owner) calls this, tx.origin will be the victim's address
        // and msg.sender will be this MaliciousRelay contract.
        // The targetWallet.transferTo will then be called with tx.origin == owner.
        targetWallet.transferTo(attacker, _amount);
    }

    receive() external payable {} // To receive funds if necessary
}
The relay itself is simple. The important property is the call chain: owner (EOA) -> MaliciousRelay -> VulnerableWallet. tx.origin remains the owner throughout.
Testing tips
  • Deploy vulnerable wallet with owner having initial funds.
  • Deploy MaliciousRelay from attacker account targeting the wallet.
  • Have the owner call phishingAttack and assert balances changed as expected.
Misconception check: The relay does not need special privileges on the vulnerable wallet to succeed if tx.origin is used for authorization.

screens.title: Patching: Use msg.sender and onlyOwner
screens.narratorSegment: To fix the tx. origin vulnerability we replace origin-based checks with msg. sender-based authorization and an explicit modifier. The SecureAccess pattern stores the owner at construction and provides an onlyOwner modifier that requires msg. sender to equal owner. Applying this modifier to withdraw functions ensures only the immediate caller that holds owner privileges can perform the operation. This blocks the relay attack because when the malicious contract calls the target, msg. sender will be the relay address, not the owner. Open-source libraries like OpenZeppelin provide audited Ownable contracts that implement this pattern and also include ownership transfer functions for safe admin changes. A concrete example in tests: after patching, deploying the same MaliciousRelay and simulating owner interaction should no longer transfer funds; the call should either do nothing or revert. A common misconception is to think adding extra require checks everywhere is sufficient; prefer a clear modifier to centralize access control and reduce the chance of missing a protection. Takeaway: explicit, centralized authorization using msg. sender is the correct fix for this class of vulnerability. Patching: Use msg.sender and onlyOwner means centralize authorization with msg.sender checks and an onlyowner modifier or audited ownable implementation.. In practical terms, fix the vulnerability with immediate caller checks and modifiers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Secure Access
SecureAccess.sol (pattern)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SecureAccess {
    address public owner;

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
    }

    modifier onlyOwner() {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call this function");
        _;
    }

    function withdrawFunds() public onlyOwner {
        // ... logic to withdraw funds ...
    }
}
This pattern ensures only the immediate caller with ownership can execute sensitive logic. Use audited libraries for production and centralize ownership checks to reduce mistakes.
Why this works
  • msg.sender reflects the direct caller, so a relay contract calling the target will have msg.sender equal to the relay, not the owner.
  • Only explicit, centralized checks reduce the chance of missing a protection in another function.
Key Takeaway
Authorize the caller you intend to trust and keep that logic in a modifier or an audited library.

screens.title: Testing the tx.origin Exploit
screens.narratorSegment: Testing is the final arbiter of whether your fix works. The provided test template demonstrates a two-stage approach. First, reproduce the exploit against the vulnerable contract. Deploy VulnerableWalletTxOrigin with the owner having an initial balance, deploy MaliciousRelay by the attacker, then have the owner call the relay’s phishing function. Assert the owner’s internal balance in the wallet decreased while the attacker’s increased. Second, confirm the patched version prevents the same sequence. Replace the vulnerable contract with a version that uses msg. sender or onlyOwner, then repeat the attack scenario expecting a revert. The test skeleton uses the Hardhat framework and the connect pattern to simulate owner and attacker signers. A subtle point: when you simulate the owner calling the relay, the tx. origin is the owner and msg. sender is the relay; this is exactly the attacker scenario. A common misconception is trusting unit tests that only call functions from EOAs; you must also test relay-based calls and large-data scenarios for DoS. The takeaway is to include attacker-style tests in your CI so regressions are caught early. Testing the tx.origin Exploit means simulate both the relay exploit and the patched contract; use connect() to run calls from different signers and assert expected reverts or balance changes.. In practical terms, write unit tests that reproduce the phishing attack and validate the patch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Tx.origin Tests
Test skeleton (excerpt)
const { expect } = require("chai");
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

describe("Tx.origin Vulnerability", function () {
  let VulnerableWalletTxOrigin, vulnerableWalletTxOrigin;
  let MaliciousRelay, maliciousRelay;
  let owner, attacker;

  beforeEach(async function () {
    [owner, attacker] = await ethers.getSigners();

    VulnerableWalletTxOrigin = await ethers.getContractFactory("VulnerableWalletTxOrigin", owner);
    vulnerableWalletTxOrigin = await VulnerableWalletTxOrigin.deploy({ value: ethers.utils.parseEther("1") });

    MaliciousRelay = await ethers.getContractFactory("MaliciousRelay", attacker);
    maliciousRelay = await MaliciousRelay.deploy(vulnerableWalletTxOrigin.address);
  });

  it("Should demonstrate tx.origin phishing attack", async function () {
    const transferAmount = ethers.utils.parseEther("0.5");
    await maliciousRelay.connect(owner).phishingAttack(owner.address, transferAmount);
    expect(await vulnerableWalletTxOrigin.getBalance(attacker.address)).to.equal(transferAmount);
  });
});
This example shows how to reproduce the exploit. Extend it by asserting owner balances and testing the patched contract expecting reverts.
Testing checklist
  • Simulate owner calling the relay to reproduce the exploit.

screens.title: Front-running
screens.narratorSegment: Front-running happens when an attacker sees a pending transaction in the mempool and then submits their own transaction with a higher gas price so miners or sequencers include it first. In decentralized exchanges, a large pending buy order is a canonical target: an attacker buys first, pushes the price up, and then sells to the victim’s order for profit. Another common example is auction bids: an attacker can observe a high bid and submit a slightly higher bid immediately before the auction closes. Mitigations reduce the attacker’s ability to observe or exploit pending data. A commit-reveal scheme hides the sensitive value by having users first commit a hash of their value and reveal the real value in a later transaction. Batching or delaying execution groups many actions so an attacker cannot target a single pending operation. Trusted relayers or sequencers can order transactions to avoid front-running, but they introduce centralization trade-offs. For trades, specifying max slippage or price limits prevents attackers from pushing prices beyond an acceptable range. A common misconception is believing private mempools or encrypted transactions fully solve front-running; they reduce exposure but may add trust or complexity. The takeaway is to match mitigation to the threat model: commit-reveal for secrecy, batching for fairness, and slippage limits for financial operations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Front-running
What is front-running?
Front-running is a mempool-based attack where an observer submits a competing transaction with a higher fee to get it mined first, gaining an advantage from the original transaction.
Example — DEX trade
A large buy order is visible to bots. Attacker buys first at lower price, then the victim’s order fills at a higher price, letting the attacker profit.
Example — Auction
Seeing a high bid before settlement enables an attacker to submit an even higher bid just before closing.
Mitigation overview
  • Commit-Reveal: hide details by committing a hash, then reveal later.
  • Batching/Delaying: group actions or delay execution to remove single-transaction exposure.
  • Trusted relayer/sequencer: centralize ordering with trade-offs.
  • Slippage limits: cap acceptable price movement for trades.
Misconception: a single mitigation fits all cases. Choose based on whether secrecy, fairness, or decentralization is your primary requirement.

screens.title: Commit-Reveal Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: The commit-reveal scheme is a practical, well-understood mitigation against front-running. The process has two clear steps. First, users submit a commit transaction containing a hash of their secret data plus a nonce. This commit reveals nothing about the underlying value in the mempool. Second, after the commit phase ends or a minimum number of blocks pass, users submit a reveal transaction that includes the original value and nonce. The contract verifies the hash matches the earlier commit and then executes the action. The concrete benefit is that front-runners cannot produce a valid competing transaction because they don’t know the original value until reveal time. A common misconception is that commit-reveal removes all timing risk; it prevents direct observation of values but requires careful phase timing and handling of missing reveals. For auctions, make sure a reveal window exists and handle absent reveals (for example, mark commits as forfeited). For testing, simulate both honest reveals and adversarial attempts to guess or abort reveals. The takeaway is that commit-reveal trades a little complexity and latency for secrecy, which can be the right trade when front-running poses financial risk.

keyIdea.text: Two-phase scheme: commit a hash to hide data, then reveal later to prove the value and execute safely.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Commit-Reveal
Process steps
1. Commit
User submits a hash of their secret plus nonce. The contract stores the commit without revealing the secret.
2. Wait / Window
A short waiting period or batch ensures commits are collected before reveals.
3. Reveal
User sends the clear value and nonce. The contract verifies the hash and then executes the intended action.
Notes & pitfalls
  • Handle missing reveals: decide whether to cancel commits or penalize non-reveals.
  • Ensure reveal windows are long enough for honest users but short enough to limit latency.
  • Remember this adds complexity and gas overhead; evaluate cost vs benefit.
Misconception: commit-reveal eliminates all front-running. It obscures values but needs correct phase management to be effective.

screens.title: Denial-of-Service (DoS) in Smart Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: Denial-of-Service attacks aim to make a contract or function unusable. Two common sources are unbounded loops and blocking external calls. For unbounded loops, if a contract iterates over a dynamic array whose size an attacker can grow, the gas cost of the loop can exceed the block limit, causing the function to revert or never be callable. The payAllUsers example in the source shows this vulnerability: distributing funds by iterating an array divides the payable amount and transfers to every address, which becomes infeasible if the array grows large. Blocking external calls are similar: if the contract sends funds to recipients in a loop and one recipient is a malicious contract that always reverts, it can prevent further transfers. A strong defense is the pull-over-push pattern: instead of sending funds automatically, let users withdraw their own funds. This removes the need for a global loop and prevents a single failing recipient from blocking others. Pagination and processing in batches also limit per-transaction work so operations remain within gas limits. A misconception is thinking that adding gas increases fixes the issue; blocks have hard limits and transactions can still fail. The takeaway is to design payment and data-processing flows so no single participant can deny service to all others.

keyIdea.title: DoS root causes
keyIdea.text: Avoid unbounded loops and push payments; prefer pull-over-push, batching, and pagination to preserve availability.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Denial-of-Service
Gas Limit DoS example
// Vulnerable to DoS if `users` array grows too large
function payAllUsers(address[] memory users) public payable {
    for (uint i = 0; i < users.length; i++) {
        payable(users[i]).transfer(msg.value / users.length);
    }
}
If an attacker adds many entries to users, the loop may exceed the block gas limit, making this function unusable. Similarly, if any transfer reverts, it can block the entire operation.
Defenses
  • Pull over push: let users withdraw funds themselves.
  • Pagination / Batching: process in limited-size chunks to bound per-transaction gas.
  • Design for failed external calls: assume external transfers can revert and write state so failures don't block progress.
Misconception: making transfers in a single transaction is simpler. It is, but it increases DoS surface and gives attackers a single point to block.

screens.title: Secure Design Patterns and Testing Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: This final lesson in the sequence ties the patterns together and gives a compact testing checklist. Use the following patterns in combination: centralize authorization with msg. sender and onlyOwner; prefer pull-over-push for payments to avoid blocking recipients; apply commit-reveal where secrecy matters; and paginate or batch large operations to bound gas. Architecturally, keep permission checks minimal and in one place so they are easy to audit. For testing, include these specific scenarios: unauthorized caller attempts, malicious relay replication of the tx. origin phishing flow, stress tests that populate large arrays to observe gas behavior, and failure-simulation tests where external calls revert. When simulating the relay, deploy a simple malicious contract and have the owner call the relay in test to reproduce the exploit. For DoS, push many entries into a collection and attempt the loop to verify it either reverts or is intentionally paginated. A common misconception is that adding logging or extra require checks is sufficient; tests that replicate attacker behavior are the true proof. The core takeaway is that patterns and tests together create resilience: design to limit trust and verify by mimicking attackers.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.6 › Patterns & Tests
Recommended patterns
Authorization
Centralize with msg.sender checks and an onlyOwner modifier or audited Ownable implementation.
Payments
Prefer pull-over-push: users withdraw their balances to avoid blocking and allow gas-bounded operations.
Front-running
Use commit-reveal or batching for time-sensitive values; use slippage for DEX trades.
Scalability
Implement pagination and batch processing to keep per-transaction gas bounded.
Testing checklist
  1. Unauthorized calls should revert with the expected error string.
  2. Deploy and simulate MaliciousRelay calling vulnerable functions.
  3. Populate arrays to stress loops and verify batch pagination works.
  4. Simulate external call failures to ensure state remains consistent.
Ask during code review: what can an attacker force into being the immediate caller, and what happens if many accounts are added to this list?

In this lesson we explore three practical classes of smart contract risks: incorrect access control that uses the wrong caller identity, front-running attacks where an adversary races transactions, and denial-of-service vectors that make functions unusable. You will learn the concrete difference between msg. sender and tx. origin, why using tx. origin for authorization can be exploited via a phishing-style malicious relay, and how to use msg. sender and established patterns like onlyOwner to avoid that trap. We’ll then examine front-running in time-sensitive operations and walk through mitigations such as commit-reveal, batching or delaying execution, and limiting slippage for trades. Finally, we’ll investigate DoS attacks driven by unbounded loops or blocking external calls and practical defenses like pagination, pull-over-push withdrawals, and designing state changes to tolerate failing external calls. Each topic includes a code example and testing approach so you can both fix vulnerable code and write tests that assert the protection. By the end, you should be able to identify these issues in code, patch them safely, and structure tests that prove the contract resists simple exploit scenarios. Ask yourself: which caller identity are you trusting, and could an intermediate contract be tricking your logic?

By the end of this lesson you will be able to identify and fix common access control mistakes, understand and mitigate front-running, and design contracts that resist denial-of-service vectors. First, you will clearly distinguish msg. sender from tx. origin and explain why relying on tx. origin for authorization is unsafe. Second, you will name at least two front-running mitigations and reason about when to apply commit-reveal versus batching or slippage limits. Third, you will recognize DoS patterns such as unbounded loops and blocking external calls and apply defenses like pagination and pull-over-push. Finally, you will implement tests that simulate these attacks: use unauthorized accounts to assert reverts, deploy a malicious relay contract to reproduce a tx. origin phishing exploit, and create large data sets to verify loops can exceed gas limits. These skills matter because they let you move from reactive fixes to proactive design: you can write contracts that remain usable under adversarial conditions and write tests that demonstrate resilience. Think about your current contracts and ask: which functions would fail if an attacker filled an array, or if a user was tricked into calling a malicious relay?

This second objectives slide focuses on practical habits you should adopt. First, always prefer msg. sender for immediate caller checks and wrap sensitive functions with a clear modifier, for example an onlyOwner pattern. Second, when a function’s correctness depends on secrecy or timing—like auction bids or large DEX trades—apply a commit-reveal workflow or batching so attackers cannot observe and profit from pending transactions. Third, use pull-over-push withdrawals and guard loops against unbounded growth to prevent DoS. Finally, integrate tests that mimic an attacker: deploy a malicious relay contract that calls your vulnerable function when the victim interacts, and run large-scale tests that populate arrays to see whether operations run out of gas. These behaviors reduce the chance that a design decision creates a simple exploit. When reviewing code, ask: who am I trusting, what data is visible in the mempool, and what happens if an external call reverts?

Let’s clearly define the two caller identities you’ll see in Solidity. msg. sender is the address that immediately invoked the current call. If an EOA calls your contract directly, msg. sender is that EOA. But if a contract calls your contract, msg. sender is the intermediary contract. tx. origin, by contrast, is the original externally owned account that began the entire transaction chain. That difference matters because tx. origin remains the same through nested calls, which means a malicious contract can cause tx. origin to be an honest user while msg. sender is the attacker-controlled contract. A concrete example: a contract that uses require(tx. origin == owner) to protect a withdraw function can be drained if the owner is tricked into calling a malicious relay. The relay’s call will have msg. sender equal to the relay, but tx. origin equal to the owner, satisfying the check. A common misconception is thinking tx. origin is a stronger identity because it ties back to the original user; in fact it opens a phishing vector because you no longer control who can place an intermediary contract between the EOA and your contract. The safe rule is: authorize the immediate caller you expect. Use msg. sender or explicit modifiers like onlyOwner, and test your assumptions by deploying a relay contract in your test suite. Now we examine a concrete vulnerable contract that uses tx. origin for an authorization check. The VulnerableWalletTxOrigin contract sets owner to the deployer and then requires tx. origin == owner for a transfer function. That condition looks like it protects the owner, but it doesn't restrict intermediate callers. An attacker can deploy a separate malicious relay contract that calls transferTo on the vulnerable wallet. If the owner is tricked into calling the relay’s function—perhaps by interacting with a dApp or a phishing link—the transaction's tx. origin stays the owner, while msg. sender becomes the relay contract. The relay then calls transferTo and passes the tx. origin check, enabling funds to move to the attacker. This is more than theory: we can reproduce it in tests by deploying the vulnerable wallet with an initial balance, deploying the malicious relay by the attacker, then having the owner call the relay's phishing function. The test should assert that the attacker's balance in the wallet increases and the owner's decreases. A common misconception is thinking that only contracts can be malicious; EOAs can be tricked into initiating a transaction chain that hands access to an attacker. The takeaway is to never rely on tx. origin for authorization and to write tests that intentionally try the relay scenario.

Next we inspect the malicious relay contract used to trick an owner into authorizing a transfer. The relay receives the target vulnerable wallet address at deployment and stores the attacker as the deployer. Its phishingAttack function simply calls the vulnerable wallet’s transfer function while the owner, acting as the origin, triggers the relay. This demonstrates the exact sequence in which tx. origin remains the owner while msg. sender is the relay. In practice, an attacker will try to induce the owner to call the relay—for example by promising some benefit or by social engineering—so tests should simulate the owner calling the relay directly. You should be able to reproduce this attack in unit tests: deploy the vulnerable wallet with an initial balance, deploy the malicious relay by the attacker, then call phishingAttack connected as the owner. Assertions must check that the attacker’s wallet balance increased inside the vulnerable wallet and the owner’s decreased. A misconception to avoid is thinking only on-chain bots can perform these steps; the owner themselves can trigger the chain when interacting with a malicious dApp. The defensive lesson is to assume intermediaries can exist and to protect the immediate caller, not the origin.

A common misconception is that adding logging or extra require checks is sufficient; tests that replicate attacker behavior are the true proof. The core takeaway is that patterns and tests together create resilience: design to limit trust and verify by mimicking attackers.

These three concise reminders capture the defensive rules you’ll use again and again. First, prefer msg. sender for authorization and centralize access control in modifiers or audited libraries — never use tx. origin for authentication. Second, anticipate mempool-based attacks by applying commit-reveal, batching, or slippage limits depending on whether secrecy or decentralization is most important. Third, design for availability: avoid unbounded loops and push payments, use pagination and pull-over-push, and write tests that simulate attacker behavior. Carry these practices into your code reviews and CI tests so the protections remain effective as your contracts evolve.
